screens.title: Lambda Advanced Topics & Integration
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we bring Lambda beyond single-function demos into production-ready patterns. You will learn how A P I Gateway acts as the front door to expose Lambda as REST or HTTP endpoints, how DynamoDB Streams make your database changes first-class events, and how versioning and aliases give you safe, reversible deployments. We also cover infrastructure-as-code with the AWS Serverless Application Model and the Serverless Framework so you can define, build, and deploy complete serverless stacks. For example, you will see how an A P I Gateway request becomes a JSON event that invokes Lambda, and how a stream record with OldImage and NewImage allows immediate, targeted processing. These ideas matter because real systems require safe releases, observability, and repeatable deployments. As you follow the upcoming walk-throughs, you will practice a SAM template that declares a function and an A P I event, use the SAM CLI to build and deploy, and test a working endpoint in your browser. By the end you should be able to integrate Lambda into web and event-driven flows and manage updates safely with versions and aliases. Which integration would you pick first for your app and why?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Lambda Advanced Topics
Lambda Advanced Topics & Integration
Building robust serverless applications with API Gateway, DynamoDB Streams, versioning, and SAM

This chapter ties together the most common integration patterns you will use in production: exposing functions as APIs, reacting to database changes in real time, and deploying safely with infrastructure-as-code. We focus on practical patterns you can test with the SAM CLI.

In this lesson
API Integration
Expose Lambda via API Gateway using proxy or non-proxy integration.
Streams & Events
Use DynamoDB Streams to trigger real-time processing from table changes.
Safe Deployments
Manage versions and aliases for blue/green or canary rollouts.
Visual Concept
Requests → Events → Functions → Results
Front Door
API Gateway accepts HTTP and converts it to a JSON event for Lambda.
Event Source
DynamoDB Streams capture item changes you can process immediately.
Explore Key Topics
API Gateway Integration
Learn proxy vs non-proxy and how requests map to Lambda events.
DynamoDB Streams
Capture OldImage and NewImage to build real-time pipelines.
SAM & Deployments
Define functions, events, and policies in a single YAML template.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these lessons you will integrate Lambda with A P I Gateway to produce RESTful endpoints, configure and respond to DynamoDB Streams for real-time processing, and manage safe releases using Lambda versioning and aliases. You will also be able to declare and deploy serverless stacks using the AWS Serverless Application Model or the Serverless Framework. For example, after the hands-on activity you will initialize a SAM project, inspect the template that defines an AWS::Serverless::Function and its Api event, build the code, and run a guided deploy to produce a public endpoint you can open in your browser. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: integration, event-driven processing, lifecycle management, and deployment automation. These skills reduce manual configuration errors, let your application react to data changes immediately, and allow fast rollbacks when a release fails. Think about a small web service that needs a public A P I, a DynamoDB table for data, and an automated pipeline to deploy updates safely. That scenario ties every objective together and shows why each skill matters.

screens.title: API Gateway as the 'Front Door' for Lambda
screens.narratorSegment: A P I Gateway serves as the front door to your serverless APIs. At a conceptual level it accepts an HTTP request, performs any configured authorization, and then converts the HTTP data—method, headers, query string, path parameters, and body—into a JSON event that your Lambda function can receive. This mapping can be direct and complete, as in Lambda proxy integration, or it can be partial and explicit with non-proxy integration where you map specific parameters. Understanding this mapping matters because it affects how much code you write inside A P I Gateway versus inside Lambda. For example, with proxy integration your function receives the entire request and is responsible for parsing path parameters and bodies; that simplifies Gateway configuration and is recommended for most cases. A common misconception is that A P I Gateway always hides the HTTP details: it does not. When you use non-proxy integration, Gateway can map and validate fields before invoking Lambda, which can reduce code complexity but increases configuration work. In practice you will choose proxy integration to move logic into code and use non-proxy when you need Gateway-level transformations. Key takeaway: pick the integration type that balances operational simplicity and configuration reuse, then test with a simple GET request and confirm the Lambda event shape matches your handler expectations.

keyIdea.title: Gateway → JSON Event
keyIdea.text: API Gateway converts HTTP requests into JSON events; proxy integration passes the whole request to Lambda, while non-proxy maps fields explicitly.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › API Gateway Integration
Concept Overview
  • API Gateway accepts HTTP and converts it into a JSON event for Lambda.
  • Proxy integration forwards the full request; non-proxy requires explicit mapping.
  • Choose proxy for simplicity, non-proxy for heavy request validation in Gateway.
Concrete Example
A GET /hello?name=Cohortia request becomes a JSON event and the function returns a JSON body which API Gateway maps to an HTTP response.
Key Takeaway

Use proxy integration for most apps to reduce Gateway configuration and keep request parsing in your code.

Integration Diagram (logical)
Client HTTP Request → API Gateway (auth, throttling, mapping)
API Gateway invokes Lambda with a JSON event. The event includes method, headers, query parameters, path parameters, and the body.
Lambda processes the event and returns a response object that Gateway converts back to HTTP for the client.
Common Mistake
Assuming API Gateway hides HTTP complexity. If you rely on proxy integration you must parse path and query parameters in your function; non-proxy can do some mapping for you.

screens.title: Lambda Proxy Integration vs Non-Proxy Integration
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding between Lambda proxy integration and non-proxy integration is an important architectural choice. Proxy integration hands the entire HTTP request to your Lambda function as a JSON event. This keeps Gateway configuration minimal and moves parsing, validation, and error handling into your codebase. Non-proxy integration lets A P I Gateway map specific parts of the request to method request parameters or directly to the function input, which can reduce code complexity for common mapping patterns and centralize validation at the Gateway layer. A practical example: if your A P I needs simple routing and the function already includes input validation and parsing, proxy integration will speed development. If you want strict request validation, parameter mapping, and response templates enforced before the function runs, non-proxy makes sense. A common misconception is that non-proxy is always safer; in reality it can increase configuration overhead and make troubleshooting harder if mappings are complex. When you expect rapid iteration or prefer single-source logic, choose proxy. When organizational policies require Gateway-level validation or you want to reuse mapping across many functions, consider non-proxy. Understand the trade-off and align it with your operational practices.

keyIdea.title: Trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Proxy integration simplifies Gateway configuration and centralizes parsing in code; non-proxy centralizes request mapping and validation in API Gateway at the cost of more configuration.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Proxy vs Non-Proxy
Lambda Proxy Integration
Sends the entire HTTP request as a JSON event to Lambda. Function must parse method, headers, path, query string, and body.
  • Pros: simple Gateway setup, rapid iteration, single place for parsing and validation.
  • Cons: function must handle all HTTP concerns; repeated logic may be duplicated across functions.
Example: GET /hello?name=Cohortia becomes an event where handler reads event['queryStringParameters']['name'].
Non-Proxy Integration
API Gateway maps specific request elements to invocation payloads and can validate or transform inputs before calling Lambda.
  • Pros: centralized mapping and validation, reuse of mapping templates.
  • Cons: additional Gateway configuration and potential complexity when mappings change.
Example: Map a path parameter to a JSON property the function expects, avoiding parsing in code.
Decision Checklist
Prefer proxy when you want fast development and code-driven parsing.
Prefer non-proxy when you need common validation and reusable mappings across APIs.
Remember: maintenance and troubleshooting differ depending on where logic lives.

screens.title: DynamoDB Streams: Event Source for Real-Time Processing
screens.narratorSegment: DynamoDB Streams captures a time-ordered sequence of item-level modifications—each INSERT, MODIFY, or REMOVE—made to a table and retains those records for up to 24 hours. When a stream is enabled, you can attach a Lambda function as a trigger. The function receives an event object that contains a list of stream records. Each record includes metadata such as eventName, eventSource, and a dynamodb object that carries OldImage and NewImage representations of the item when available. This structure lets you react to exact changes: for example, on a new user INSERT you can provision resources or send a welcome email; on MODIFY you can update a search index using the NewImage; on REMOVE you can perform cleanup based on the OldImage. A common misconception is that streams provide long-term change history: they do not. They are a short-lived event source intended for immediate processing and downstream propagation. When designing real-time pipelines, account for the 24-hour window and make processing idempotent because records can be retried. Ultimately, DynamoDB Streams turns your table into an event source that enables reactive architectures without polling.

keyIdea.title: Short-lived, Item-level Events
keyIdea.text: DynamoDB Streams capture INSERT, MODIFY, REMOVE events with OldImage and NewImage for up to 24 hours and trigger Lambda for real-time processing.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › DynamoDB Streams
What Streams Provide
  • Time-ordered item-level changes: INSERT, MODIFY, REMOVE.
  • Each record contains eventName, eventSource, and a dynamodb object with OldImage and NewImage.
  • Retention is short—records are available for up to 24 hours.
Use case: Trigger a Lambda on new sign-ups (INSERT) to send a welcome email or provision resources.
Design Notes
  • Make handlers idempotent: retries may occur.
  • Do not assume long-term history; persist important events to durable stores if needed.
  • Use OldImage and NewImage to compute deltas and perform targeted updates.
Common Mistake: Treating streams as an audit log. They are a transient event stream designed for immediate downstream processing.
Key Takeaway

DynamoDB Streams turn table changes into events you can process in real time, enabling responsive systems for indexes, notifications, and analytics.

screens.title: Parsing a DynamoDB Stream Event in Lambda
screens.narratorSegment: When a Lambda is triggered by a DynamoDB Stream it receives an event with a list of records. Each record tells you whether it was an INSERT, MODIFY, or REMOVE and includes the dynamodb object with OldImage and NewImage when applicable. A minimal handler iterates over event['Records'], checks eventName to decide what to do, and inspects NewImage or OldImage to retrieve item attributes. In practice you convert the DynamoDB attribute map into plain types before processing and design logic to be idempotent. For example, on INSERT you might create an index entry using the NewImage. A common misconception is that each record contains only the changed attributes: depending on your stream view type, NewImage can include the full item. Make parsing robust to missing OldImage or NewImage fields and protect against partial failures by batching and checkpointing properly. The code example shown illustrates a simple Python handler that iterates records, detects eventName, and reads NewImage attributes. Use this pattern as a starting point and add error handling, logging, and deduplication for production workloads. Parsing a DynamoDB Stream Event in Lambda means loop over event.records, check eventname, then use oldimage/newimage to drive idempotent processing logic.. In practical terms, walkthrough of the event structure and a minimal handler pattern. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Iterate, Inspect, Process
keyIdea.text: Loop over event.Records, check eventName, then use OldImage/NewImage to drive idempotent processing logic.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Stream Handler
Handler Pattern
  • Iterate event['Records'] and inspect each record's eventName.
  • Use NewImage for the new state, OldImage when needed for cleanup or diffs.
  • Keep processing idempotent and log meaningful context for retries.
Concrete Example (Python)
def lambda_handler(event, context):
  # event contains Records from DynamoDB Streams
  for record in event.get('Records', []):
    event_name = record.get('eventName')
    dynamodb = record.get('dynamodb', {})
    new_image = dynamodb.get('NewImage')
    old_image = dynamodb.get('OldImage')

    if event_name == 'INSERT' and new_image:
      # convert DynamoDB attribute map to values and process
      user_id = new_image.get('userId', {}).get('S')
      # perform action: send welcome email or provision resources
    elif event_name == 'MODIFY':
      # compare old_image and new_image if present
      pass
    elif event_name == 'REMOVE':
      # cleanup using old_image
      pass
Note: convert attribute maps and handle missing fields safely.
Check Your Understanding
What would you do differently if NewImage only contains changed attributes instead of the full item? How would you ensure idempotency?

screens.title: Lambda Versioning: Immutable Snapshots
screens.narratorSegment: Lambda versioning lets you publish immutable snapshots of your function code and configuration. Each published version has a unique ARN so that callers can invoke a specific snapshot without being affected by later updates. This is essential for stability when different clients or environments require predictable behavior. For instance, you might publish Version 1 of a function that your production alias refers to; developers can continue iterating in $LATEST without impacting the published version. The main benefit is reproducibility: a version guarantees that the code and configured settings will not change. A common misconception is that versions automatically manage traffic. They do not. Versions are immutable references; aliases are used to provide stable names and to manage traffic between versions. Use versions to mark milestones such as releases or hotfixes and couple them with aliases or deployment automation for safe rollouts. Publishing versions is a low-risk step that buys you rollback capability and clearer traceability in logs and monitoring. Lambda Versioning: Immutable Snapshots means publishing a lambda version creates an immutable snapshot you can invoke directly and use as a stable baseline for deployments and rollbacks.. In practical terms, publish immutable function versions to stabilize production behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Lambda Versioning
What a Version Is
A published, immutable snapshot of code and configuration. Each version has a unique ARN and cannot be changed after publish.
Why Versions Matter
  • Provide stability for production clients.
  • Enable traceable releases and easier rollbacks when combined with aliases.
Example Workflow
Publish Version 1, test, then publish Version 2 for new features. Versions are referenced by ARN for stable invocation.
Misconception: Versions change traffic. They do not. To change traffic you update an alias that points to a version.

screens.title: Aliases and Safe Deployment Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Aliases point to specific Lambda versions and provide a stable name your clients can call. By updating an alias to reference a new version, you can switch traffic without changing client code. Weighted aliases let you split traffic between versions, enabling canary deployments where only a small percentage of users see the new version initially. A recommended rollout uses these steps: publish the new version; create or update an alias to reference both versions with a weight (for example 10% new, 90% old); monitor metrics and logs for errors or latency; then gradually increase the weight to 100% once confidence is high. If a problem appears at any point, set the alias back to the previous version or adjust weights for an immediate rollback. Blue/green is similar but typically uses separate aliases or endpoints to switch all traffic at once. A common mistake is failing to monitor both versions while weights are split — always verify application-level health and error budgets during a canary. Aliases combined with versions give you safe, reversible deployments that minimize user impact. Aliases and Safe Deployment Strategies means use aliases and weighted routing to shift traffic gradually to new versions and enable rapid rollback when problems occur.. In practical terms, use aliases and weighted routing to perform canary or blue/green rollouts and instant rollback. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › Aliases & Rollouts
Canary Rollout Steps
  1. Publish new version (e.g., Version 2).
  2. Create or update an alias and set weights (10% to Version 2, 90% to Version 1).
  3. Monitor logs and metrics for the alias.
  4. If healthy, increase weight to 100%; if not, revert alias back to Version 1.
Example: Create a PROD alias that initially points to Version 1. After publishing Version 2, update PROD alias weights to test new code with a small portion of traffic.
Practical Checks
  • Monitor error rates and latencies for both versions during weighted routing.
  • Ensure logs indicate which version served requests for fast debugging.
  • Keep aliases consistent across environments for predictable deployments.

screens.title: AWS Serverless Application Model (SAM)
screens.narratorSegment: AWS SAM is an open-source framework that extends CloudFormation with a simplified syntax for defining serverless resources. Instead of writing verbose CloudFormation templates you declare higher-level resources like AWS::Serverless::Function and specify Events, Policies, Handler, and Runtime in a concise way. SAM enables a single template to define a Lambda, its A P I Gateway event, and required IAM permissions, and the SAM CLI provides commands to build, test locally, and deploy the entire application. This matters because it removes repetitive configuration and makes deployments reproducible across environments. The Serverless Framework offers a broader multi-cloud approach with plugins, but SAM is tightly integrated with AWS tooling and CloudFormation. A common misconception is that SAM hides CloudFormation entirely; it does not. SAM templates are transformed into CloudFormation and you still see stacks and resources in the console. Use SAM when you prefer a focused serverless experience that still produces standard CloudFormation stacks and allows guided deployments via sam deploy --guided. AWS Serverless Application Model (SAM) means sam provides higher-level serverless resource types and a cli to build, test, and deploy serverless applications as cloudformation stacks.. In practical terms, a framework that extends cloudformation to simplify serverless definitions and deployments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: A SAM template declares functions, events, and policies so the entire serverless stack can be built and deployed consistently.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.4 › SAM Template
Provided YAML Snippet
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31
Description: A simple API Gateway + Lambda function

Resources:
  MyApiFunction:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::Function
    Properties:
      Handler: app.lambda_handler
      Runtime: python3.9
      CodeUri: s3://my-code-bucket/my-app.zip
      MemorySize: 128
      Timeout: 30
      Policies:
        - AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole
      Events:
        Api:
          Type: Api
          Properties:
            Path: /hello
            Method: GET
Key Properties Explained
  • Handler and Runtime tell Lambda how to run your code.
  • CodeUri points to the function package location.
  • Events.Api defines an API Gateway endpoint that invokes the function.
Practical Tip

Use sam deploy --guided to capture deployment preferences and create a CloudFormation stack that matches this template.

screens.title: Serverless Framework vs SAM and Operational Considerations
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter mentions both the AWS Serverless Application Model and the Serverless Framework. SAM is tightly integrated with AWS and simplifies serverless definitions by extending CloudFormation, whereas the Serverless Framework supports multiple cloud providers and a rich plugin ecosystem. Choose SAM when you want native CloudFormation stacks and a CLI focused on AWS; choose Serverless Framework if you require multi-cloud support or specific third-party plugins. Operationally, both approaches require you to manage IAM policies for functions. The SAM example includes AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole to allow basic execution. When you declare policies in templates be explicit about least privilege to reduce risk. Also plan for cleanup: the hands-on activity shows deleting a CloudFormation stack to remove deployed resources. A common misconception is that frameworks manage runtime policies automatically; they provide options, but you must still review the generated policies and roles. Finally, ensure your deployment process includes monitoring and rollback steps, especially when using aliases and staged rollouts. The right tool depends on your organization's needs and the level of provider coupling you accept. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we bring Lambda beyond single-function demos into production-ready patterns. You will learn how A P I Gateway acts as the front door to expose Lambda as REST or HTTP endpoints, how DynamoDB Streams make your database changes first-class events, and how versioning and aliases give you safe, reversible deployments. We also cover infrastructure-as-code with the AWS Serverless Application Model and the Serverless Framework so you can define, build, and deploy complete serverless stacks. For example, you will see how an A P I Gateway request becomes a JSON event that invokes Lambda, and how a stream record with OldImage and NewImage allows immediate, targeted processing. These ideas matter because real systems require safe releases, observability, and repeatable deployments. As you follow the upcoming walk-throughs, you will practice a SAM template that declares a function and an A P I event, use the SAM CLI to build and deploy, and test a working endpoint in your browser. By the end you should be able to integrate Lambda into web and event-driven flows and manage updates safely with versions and aliases. Which integration would you pick first for your app and why?

By the end of these lessons you will integrate Lambda with A P I Gateway to produce RESTful endpoints, configure and respond to DynamoDB Streams for real-time processing, and manage safe releases using Lambda versioning and aliases. You will also be able to declare and deploy serverless stacks using the AWS Serverless Application Model or the Serverless Framework. For example, after the hands-on activity you will initialize a SAM project, inspect the template that defines an AWS::Serverless::Function and its Api event, build the code, and run a guided deploy to produce a public endpoint you can open in your browser. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: integration, event-driven processing, lifecycle management, and deployment automation. These skills reduce manual configuration errors, let your application react to data changes immediately, and allow fast rollbacks when a release fails. Think about a small web service that needs a public A P I, a DynamoDB table for data, and an automated pipeline to deploy updates safely. That scenario ties every objective together and shows why each skill matters.

This second objectives slide ties each competency to a concrete demonstration. For A P I Gateway integration, you will initialize a SAM project and deploy an A P I endpoint that returns a JSON message when visited in a browser. For DynamoDB Streams, you will enable streams on a table and create or update an item to observe the resulting stream record passed to Lambda. For versioning and aliases, you will publish a function version, create an alias, and roll traffic using weighted aliases to practice canary-style rollouts and instant rollback. For deployment, you will use sam build and sam deploy --guided to push a CloudFormation stack that includes your function, A P I event, and a basic execution policy. Each card below explains the skill, why it matters for reliability, and a simple verification step you can perform. These verifications map to the hands-on activity steps and the assessment idea so you can confirm the environment is set up correctly and the deployment can be torn down when you finish.

A P I Gateway serves as the front door to your serverless APIs. At a conceptual level it accepts an HTTP request, performs any configured authorization, and then converts the HTTP data—method, headers, query string, path parameters, and body—into a JSON event that your Lambda function can receive. This mapping can be direct and complete, as in Lambda proxy integration, or it can be partial and explicit with non-proxy integration where you map specific parameters. Understanding this mapping matters because it affects how much code you write inside A P I Gateway versus inside Lambda. For example, with proxy integration your function receives the entire request and is responsible for parsing path parameters and bodies; that simplifies Gateway configuration and is recommended for most cases. A common misconception is that A P I Gateway always hides the HTTP details: it does not. When you use non-proxy integration, Gateway can map and validate fields before invoking Lambda, which can reduce code complexity but increases configuration work. In practice you will choose proxy integration to move logic into code and use non-proxy when you need Gateway-level transformations. Key takeaway: pick the integration type that balances operational simplicity and configuration reuse, then test with a simple GET request and confirm the Lambda event shape matches your handler expectations.

Deciding between Lambda proxy integration and non-proxy integration is an important architectural choice. Proxy integration hands the entire HTTP request to your Lambda function as a JSON event. This keeps Gateway configuration minimal and moves parsing, validation, and error handling into your codebase. Non-proxy integration lets A P I Gateway map specific parts of the request to method request parameters or directly to the function input, which can reduce code complexity for common mapping patterns and centralize validation at the Gateway layer. A practical example: if your A P I needs simple routing and the function already includes input validation and parsing, proxy integration will speed development. If you want strict request validation, parameter mapping, and response templates enforced before the function runs, non-proxy makes sense. A common misconception is that non-proxy is always safer; in reality it can increase configuration overhead and make troubleshooting harder if mappings are complex. When you expect rapid iteration or prefer single-source logic, choose proxy. When organizational policies require Gateway-level validation or you want to reuse mapping across many functions, consider non-proxy. Understand the trade-off and align it with your operational practices.

DynamoDB Streams captures a time-ordered sequence of item-level modifications—each INSERT, MODIFY, or REMOVE—made to a table and retains those records for up to 24 hours. When a stream is enabled, you can attach a Lambda function as a trigger. The function receives an event object that contains a list of stream records. Each record includes metadata such as eventName, eventSource, and a dynamodb object that carries OldImage and NewImage representations of the item when available. This structure lets you react to exact changes: for example, on a new user INSERT you can provision resources or send a welcome email; on MODIFY you can update a search index using the NewImage; on REMOVE you can perform cleanup based on the OldImage. A common misconception is that streams provide long-term change history: they do not. They are a short-lived event source intended for immediate processing and downstream propagation. When designing real-time pipelines, account for the 24-hour window and make processing idempotent because records can be retried. Ultimately, DynamoDB Streams turns your table into an event source that enables reactive architectures without polling.

When a Lambda is triggered by a DynamoDB Stream it receives an event with a list of records. Each record tells you whether it was an INSERT, MODIFY, or REMOVE and includes the dynamodb object with OldImage and NewImage when applicable. A minimal handler iterates over event['Records'], checks eventName to decide what to do, and inspects NewImage or OldImage to retrieve item attributes. In practice you convert the DynamoDB attribute map into plain types before processing and design logic to be idempotent. For example, on INSERT you might create an index entry using the NewImage. A common misconception is that each record contains only the changed attributes: depending on your stream view type, NewImage can include the full item. Make parsing robust to missing OldImage or NewImage fields and protect against partial failures by batching and checkpointing properly. The code example shown illustrates a simple Python handler that iterates records, detects eventName, and reads NewImage attributes. Use this pattern as a starting point and add error handling, logging, and deduplication for production workloads. Parsing a DynamoDB Stream Event in Lambda means loop over event.records, check eventname, then use oldimage/newimage to drive idempotent processing logic.. In practical terms, walkthrough of the event structure and a minimal handler pattern. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Lambda versioning lets you publish immutable snapshots of your function code and configuration. Each published version has a unique ARN so that callers can invoke a specific snapshot without being affected by later updates. This is essential for stability when different clients or environments require predictable behavior. For instance, you might publish Version 1 of a function that your production alias refers to; developers can continue iterating in $LATEST without impacting the published version. The main benefit is reproducibility: a version guarantees that the code and configured settings will not change. A common misconception is that versions automatically manage traffic. They do not. Versions are immutable references; aliases are used to provide stable names and to manage traffic between versions. Use versions to mark milestones such as releases or hotfixes and couple them with aliases or deployment automation for safe rollouts. Publishing versions is a low-risk step that buys you rollback capability and clearer traceability in logs and monitoring. Lambda Versioning: Immutable Snapshots means publishing a lambda version creates an immutable snapshot you can invoke directly and use as a stable baseline for deployments and rollbacks.. In practical terms, publish immutable function versions to stabilize production behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Aliases point to specific Lambda versions and provide a stable name your clients can call. By updating an alias to reference a new version, you can switch traffic without changing client code. Weighted aliases let you split traffic between versions, enabling canary deployments where only a small percentage of users see the new version initially. A recommended rollout uses these steps: publish the new version; create or update an alias to reference both versions with a weight (for example 10% new, 90% old); monitor metrics and logs for errors or latency; then gradually increase the weight to 100% once confidence is high. If a problem appears at any point, set the alias back to the previous version or adjust weights for an immediate rollback. Blue/green is similar but typically uses separate aliases or endpoints to switch all traffic at once. A common mistake is failing to monitor both versions while weights are split — always verify application-level health and error budgets during a canary. AWS SAM is an open-source framework that extends CloudFormation with a simplified syntax for defining serverless resources.
